claims.text: A Pulumi blog post titled "SST Runs on the Pulumi Engine: What It Means to Build on Pulumi" exists at /blog/sst-built-on-pulumi/ and covers the engine mechanics behind SST's migration to Pulumi.
AWS CDK ties infrastructure to AWS only (AWS-only, no multi-cloud support).
Multi-cloud was nearly impossible with AWS CDK.
AWS CDK allowed developers to define infrastructure using TypeScript or Python only (table lists CDK language support as TypeScript, Python).

CDK and CloudFormation act as a code generator producing an intermediary format (YAML or JSON) that is then executed to deploy resources, so the code written is not the code running during deployment.
Pulumi supports AWS, Azure, GCP, and on-prem.
Pulumi supports any programming language.
Pulumi lets you define infrastructure in TypeScript, Python, Go, or C# and deploy across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and on-premises environments.
Pulumi deployments are faster than AWS CDK because CDK is slowed by CloudFormation while Pulumi uses direct execution.
Pulumi offers real-time debugging while CDK debugging is hard due to CloudFormation.
AWS CDK uses a CloudFormation state file for state management while Pulumi uses Pulumi-managed state.
AWS CDK secrets management is limited to AWS Secrets Manager only, whereas Pulumi supports cross-cloud secrets.
Pulumi supports custom providers and workflows for extensibility, whereas CDK extensibility is limited to the AWS ecosystem.
Pulumi treats infrastructure code as a first-class program executed directly during deployment rather than generating an intermediary format.

The Founding Engineer at SST said: "With Pulumi, the deployment process feels like a natural extension of writing code - it's intuitive and powerful and capable of advanced things that traditional IaC tools can't handle."
Pulumi Insights (product page) provides improved visibility and debugging capabilities into deployment.
Pulumi has built-in extensibility features such as custom providers and dynamic components.
With CDK/CloudFormation, SST had to resort to hacky workarounds or custom Lambda functions to achieve customization.
SST migrated from AWS CDK to Pulumi and re-implemented its higher-level components; with Pulumi the SST team was able to add support for new providers.
Pulumi Cloud Deployments documentation exists at /docs/pulumi-cloud/deployments/ describing advanced deployment workflows.
Pulumi Crosswalk for AWS simplifies "day one" tasks, documented in the AWS guide at /docs/iac/guides/clouds/aws/.
Pulumi offers an on-demand workshop titled "Getting Started with Infrastructure as Code on AWS" at /resources/getting-started-with-iac-pulumi-aws/.
Ion is the code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications, in which constructs/components are deployed using Pulumi instead of CDK and CloudFormation.
Once Ion is stable, it will be released as SST v3.
SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for its providers and deployment engine, while also bridging Terraform providers through Pulumi.
SST makes money primarily through its managed service SST Console, which is optional and includes a free tier.
SST is a framework that makes building modern full-stack applications on your infrastructure easy.
Pulumi lets SST offer a faster, more flexible, and provider-agnostic infrastructure experience.
SST v3 replaced AWS CDK and CloudFormation with an embedded Pulumi engine that calls Terraform-bridged providers to make the underlying cloud API calls.
Running `sst deploy` requires no separate Pulumi install and no Pulumi account or Pulumi Cloud dependency; the Pulumi engine ships inside the SST CLI.
SST keeps its state in an S3 bucket in the user's own AWS account rather than in Pulumi Cloud.
SST v3 is the Ion-based rewrite of SST.
The SST team has repeatedly stated, since the rewrite shipped, that SST v3 is architecturally built on the Pulumi engine.
SST is an open source TypeScript framework from the team formerly known as Serverless Stack.
SST can deploy applications to AWS and more than 150 other providers.
SST apps define infrastructure and code together in a single `sst.config.ts` file using SST components, and `sst deploy` handles provisioning end to end.
Through 2023, SST's provisioning layer was built directly on AWS CDK and CloudFormation.
In late 2023 the SST team began a rewrite code-named Ion that replaced the entire deployment layer.
Ion shipped as SST v3 in mid-2024.
Ion (SST v3 architecture) has been the only supported SST architecture since it shipped.

The SST blog post "Moving away from CDK" says: "Ion is a code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications. The constructs (or components) are defined using Terraform providers and deployed using Pulumi; as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation (CFN)."

The SST blog post "Moving away from CDK" says: "When you run `sst deploy`, those resources make a call to an embedded Pulumi engine that makes a call to their bridged Terraform provider, and this makes the AWS SDK calls to create your resources."
The SST docs "What is SST" page says: "SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for the providers and the deployment engine. And Terraform's providers are bridged through Pulumi."

Gautier Blandin's article "Terraform, Pulumi, SST: a tradeoff analysis" says SST uses the Pulumi engine under the hood to manage and provision resources, and lets users write Pulumi code in addition to SST's constructs, enabling resources with no associated SST constructs to be defined and deployed.

Kiryl Anoshka's dev.to article "SST ditches AWS CDK. Time to move on to Ion" says: "You may notice right away the imports from Pulumi. It means the whole deployment process will be built on Pulumi now."

SST's platform package.json depends on `@pulumi/pulumi`, plus first-party Pulumi providers for AWS, Cloudflare, Docker builds, and others, alongside a Pulumiverse Vercel provider (`@pulumiverse/vercel`).

The `sst/sst` repository is now `anomalyco/sst`, and its platform/package.json lists `@pulumi/pulumi`, `@pulumi/aws`, `@pulumi/cloudflare`, `@pulumi/command`, `@pulumi/docker-build`, `@pulumi/random`, `@pulumi/tls`, and `@pulumiverse/vercel` as direct dependencies.

In SST deploys, components compile into Pulumi resource declarations; the Pulumi engine diffs desired vs. actual state, builds a dependency graph and orders operations; Terraform-bridged providers translate resources into cloud API calls.
Pulumi's engine provides dependency resolution, preview and diff, state tracking, and plumbing to hundreds of provider APIs.
AWS alone exposes hundreds of resource types, each with its own create, update, and delete semantics.
Pulumi's Terraform bridge (pulumi/pulumi-terraform-bridge) is Apache-2.0 licensed.
Pulumi's Terraform bridge was built specifically to let projects like SST reuse Terraform's provider ecosystem with the Pulumi engine.
Pulumi's engine does not require a Pulumi account, a network call to Pulumi Cloud, or any Pulumi-hosted service to run.
Pulumi's Automation API lets teams embed Pulumi programs inside their own tools.
The Pulumi provider bridge lets any Pulumi user consume Terraform providers directly.
Cross-references: /docs/iac/concepts/automation-api/, /blog/any-terraform-provider/, /docs/iac/get-started/terraform/terraform-providers/ exist.
SST's Pulumi-based approach gives a production-grade provisioning engine and hundreds of cloud providers without building either from scratch.

Nitric, a cloud-agnostic application framework, states in its docs that "all of the direct deployment providers use Pulumi under the hood for their deployments," with official Nitric providers built directly on Pulumi's AWS, GCP, and Azure providers.

Defang deploys Docker Compose applications to the cloud, and its Pulumi provider is described as taking "a Compose file, translates it to a Pulumi program, and runs `pulumi up`" to provision the result.

Nitric and Defang run application deployments through the Pulumi engine rather than building their own diff, state, and provider layer, and like SST expose a narrower, more opinionated interface to users.
Most SST users never write Pulumi code and work entirely in SST's component model.
Within an SST app, resources lacking a dedicated SST construct can be defined directly as raw Pulumi resources and deployed as part of the same app.
The latest SST release, v4.17.1, went out in July 2026.
The `sst` npm package gets roughly 796,000 downloads a week (796,291 for the week of September 5-11, 2026).
SST's team page credits the same team behind opencode, an open source AI coding agent.
opencode has grown quickly since launch and now has a larger GitHub following (star count) than SST itself.
SST's dependency on the Pulumi engine hasn't changed as a result of the team's broadened attention to opencode, and SST's release cadence is unchanged.
SST does not invoke the Terraform CLI or write Terraform state; its Terraform providers are bridged through the Pulumi engine.
Pulumi Cloud offers cross-team visibility into infrastructure state; policy as code provides guardrails enforceable centrally; components allow sharing infrastructure patterns across an organization.
Anyone running SST is already running Pulumi's engine, and Pulumi Cloud, policy as code and components can be used without leaving that same engine.
SST doesn't expose cross-team visibility, policy enforcement, or infrastructure shared across more than one application on its own.

Cross-references: /blog/aws-cdk-vs-pulumi-why-sst-switched/, /docs/iac/guides/basics/how-pulumi-works/, /blog/any-terraform-provider/, /docs/iac/concepts/automation-api/ exist; the first tells SST's move off CDK from SST's side.
